title: What fatigue management training do heavy vehicle drivers and schedulers need under the HVNL?
description: Fatigue training for BFM, AFM and the new ACA-Fatigue accreditation after the HVNL reforms of August 1, 2026, including TLIF0030 and TLIF0031 units.
shortAnswer: Under the Heavy Vehicle National Law (HVNL), operators with fatigue accreditation must ensure drivers, schedulers, supervisors and managers hold fatigue units of competency from a Registered Training Organisation approved by the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator (NHVR). From August 1, 2026, Alternative Compliance Accreditation (ACA) Fatigue replaced Basic Fatigue Management (BFM) and Advanced Fatigue Management (AFM). The required units are now TLIF0030 for drivers and TLIF0031 for schedulers and managers, with earlier equivalent units still recognized.
keyTakeaways: The amended HVNL and the Heavy Vehicle Accreditation (HVA) scheme took effect on August 1, 2026; no new National Heavy Vehicle Accreditation Scheme (NHVAS) accreditation, including BFM or AFM, is being granted.
Existing BFM and AFM accreditation stays valid until it expires, is cancelled or the operator transitions, so both regimes run side by side during the transition.

Drivers under ACA Fatigue or legacy NHVAS fatigue modules need TLIF0030 Apply a fatigue risk management system (or a listed equivalent); schedulers, supervisors and managers need TLIF0031 Administer a fatigue risk management system (or an equivalent).

Schedule 1 of the Safety Management System Standard 2026 also requires fatigue induction, refreshers or reactive training after fatigue incidents, and proof that people can apply the training in practice.
Training must be delivered by an NHVR approved RTO; courses completed before August 1, 2026 remain recognized, and NHVR recommends the new units as refresher training.
jurisdiction: Australia (jurisdictions applying the Heavy Vehicle National Law)
appliesTo: Operators of fatigue-regulated heavy vehicles holding or applying for ACA Fatigue under the HVA scheme
Operators still accredited under the legacy NHVAS BFM or AFM modules
Drivers working under an operator's fatigue accreditation
Schedulers, supervisors and managers of drivers or scheduling staff

sections.heading: What changed for fatigue accreditation on August 1, 2026?

blocks.text: BFM and AFM were replaced by a single performance-based accreditation, Alternative Compliance Accreditation (ACA) Fatigue, under the new Heavy Vehicle Accreditation (HVA) scheme. The NHVR's [ACA Fatigue page](https://www.nhvr.gov.au/safety-accreditation-compliance/fatigue-management/alternative-compliance-accreditation-aca-fatigue) states that it "replaces the previous NHVAS Basic Fatigue Management (BFM) and Advanced Fatigue Management (AFM) modules and is available from 1 August 2026."

The change comes from the [Heavy Vehicle National Law Amendment Act 2025](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/html/asmade/act-2025-026) and amending regulations, which the NHVR says were passed by the Queensland Parliament on November 18, 2025. Supporting instruments, including the Safety Management System Standard 2026 and the Ministerial Standard for alternative compliance hours, were approved by transport ministers in May 2026, according to the NHVR's [HVNL reform implementation](https://www.nhvr.gov.au/law-policies/hvnl-reform-implementation) page.

Under the HVA scheme, General Safety Accreditation (GSA) against a whole of business safety management system is a prerequisite for ACA Fatigue. Operators propose Alternative Compliance Hours (ACH), which the NHVR assesses case by case using its Risk Classification System matrix, within the outer limits of the Heavy Vehicle (Fatigue Management) National Regulation. The NHVR notes that for solo drivers, work in any 24 hour period cannot exceed 15.5 hours and stationary rest must include at least 7 hours of continuous rest.

sections.heading: Do BFM and AFM still apply?

blocks.text: Yes, for operators whose accreditation has not yet expired. As at November 2026, the NHVR states that existing BFM or AFM accreditation "remains valid until it expires, is cancelled, or you choose to transition to the HVA scheme", and that no new NHVAS accreditation is being granted.

items: **Side by side operation:** NHVAS and HVA run in parallel during transition, but an operator can be accredited in only one scheme at a time ([NHVAS transition to HVA scheme](https://www.nhvr.gov.au/safety-accreditation-compliance/national-heavy-vehicle-accreditation-scheme/nhvas-transition-to-hva-scheme)).
**Extensions:** the NHVR may grant extensions to support transition, with a maximum accreditation period of three years.
**AFM drivers:** must carry a copy of the accreditation certificate, a letter of induction and a work diary unless exempt, and work to the hours on the operator's AFM certificate.
**Templates:** the NHVR publishes templated tables of hours for ACA Fatigue that include BFM equivalent and common AFM hours, to ease transition.

blocks.text: The training requirement is the same for both regimes: the NHVR's training page applies the fatigue unit requirements to operators with ACA Fatigue "or operating under legacy fatigue accreditation modules" of the NHVAS.

sections.heading: Which fatigue units of competency are required, and for whom?

blocks.text: Drivers need TLIF0030 and schedulers, supervisors and managers need TLIF0031, or a listed equivalent. The NHVR's [Training in fatigue risk management](https://www.nhvr.gov.au/safety-accreditation-compliance/fatigue-management/training-in-fatigue-risk-management) page sets out the units in its Table 1.

blocks.text: The NHVR notes that TLIF0030 and TLIF0031 "will become available through RTOs across 2026-2027" and that equivalent units remain valid in the meantime. Courses completed before August 1, 2026 continue to be recognized, but undertaking the new units as refresher training is recommended. TLIF0007 Manage a fatigue risk management system remains valid but is not required for accreditation. Training must be completed through an RTO approved by the NHVR.

blocks.title: Transition gap
blocks.text: Because the new units are being rolled out by RTOs across 2026 and 2027, an operator applying for ACA Fatigue now may legitimately rely on TLIF0005 and TLIF0006 records. Auditors will still expect the unit code, RTO and completion date for every driver and scheduler named in the accreditation.

sections.heading: What does the Safety Management System Standard 2026 add to the units?

blocks.text: It adds role knowledge, induction, refreshers and proof of applied competence on top of the unit of competency. Clause 8 of Schedule 1 to the [Safety Management System Standard 2026](https://www.ntc.gov.au/sites/default/files/assets/files/Safety%20Management%20System%20Standard%20-%20May%202026.pdf), which sets the ACA Fatigue requirements, lists these criteria:

items: Personnel involved in operating or administering the fatigue system have fatigue knowledge relevant to their role, including the operator's own policies and the physiological signs of fatigue.

Drivers can demonstrate competence with TLIF0030, and schedulers or supervisors of drivers and scheduling staff with TLIF0031, "or any previously recognised fatigue management qualification completed prior to 1 July 2018".
Fatigue responsibilities are included in inductions for new roles or new operating environments.
Knowledge is kept current "through refreshers or reactive training when fatigue-related incidents or near-misses occur".
Beyond holding a qualification, personnel can effectively apply fatigue management standards in the actual operating environment.

blocks.text: The same Schedule requires drivers to be certified fit to drive under Austroads' Assessing Fitness to Drive, including assessment for sleep disorders, at least once every three years for drivers aged 49 or under and annually for those aged 50 or over. The Standard sets no fixed refresher interval for training, so operators need to set and justify one, for example using [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

blocks.text: Executives also carry a due diligence duty for safety under the HVNL. That broader obligation is covered on the [Chain of Responsibility training requirements](/regulations/chain-of-responsibility-training-requirements) page rather than repeated here.

sections.heading: How should an operator build fatigue training that will pass an HVA audit?

blocks.text: Start from the approved hours and the fatigue risk management system, not from the course. The unit of competency proves general capability, while the HVA audit tests whether people can apply the operator's own Alternative Compliance Hours and controls.

items: List every role named in the fatigue risk management system and the unit each needs, using a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).
Check each statement of attainment against the NHVR Table 1 list, noting which staff hold older equivalent units.
Write the operator specific induction against the approved ACH table, the seven Risk Classification System principles the NHVR publishes, and the operator's fatigue controls.
Define the triggers for reactive training: fatigue incidents, near misses, roster variances and changes in operating environment.

Collect applied competence evidence through supervisor checks and work diary review, prepared as described in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the operator's Alternative Compliance Hours, fatigue controls and Schedule 1 criteria into defined knowledge points before any induction is written, then links each to the TLIF unit, the role and an assessment of applied competence. When an operator moves from BFM or AFM to ACA Fatigue, the changed hours and obligations can be traced to the content and people they affect.

faqs.q: Do drivers who completed BFM training before 2026 need to retrain?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The NHVR says courses completed before August 1, 2026 continue to be recognized, and drivers holding the listed equivalent units, such as TLIF0005 or TLIF2010, do not need the new course. The NHVR does recommend TLIF0030 or TLIF0031 as refresher training.

faqs.q: Do drivers on standard hours need fatigue units of competency?
faqs.a: The unit requirements described by the NHVR apply to operators with ACA Fatigue or legacy NHVAS fatigue accreditation. Drivers on standard hours still must not drive while impaired by fatigue, and operators still have Chain of Responsibility duties, which in practice usually include fatigue awareness training.

faqs.q: Can any RTO deliver the fatigue units?
faqs.a: No. The NHVR states that training in the fatigue units of competency must be completed through an RTO approved by the NHVR, and it publishes a list of approved RTOs.

faqs.q: What happens to BFM accreditation when it expires?
faqs.a: No new NHVAS accreditation is being granted, so an operator that wants to keep working alternative hours must apply for General Safety Accreditation and ACA Fatigue under the HVA scheme, or return to standard hours. The NHVR publishes templated tables of hours, including BFM equivalent hours, to ease that transition.
